title: Affection by the Printed Dozen
paras: Before commercial greeting cards became familiar, seasonal affection travelled chiefly through handwritten letters. A merchant addressing a distant cousin, or a [[missionary|missionary]] writing home, might spend considerable time choosing an appropriate [[salution|salutation]]. Such correspondence demanded effort; nevertheless, its personal character gave it emotional authority. The subsequent history of the greeting card would turn on whether printed words could retain that intimacy.

In Britain, cheaper postage helped [[hasten|hasten]] this transition. The celebrated Christmas card commissioned in 1843 showed a family raising glasses around a table, flanked by scenes of charitable giving. Later manufacturers developed elaborate products whose embossed borders and delicate colouring required [[painstaking|painstaking]] work. Their appeal depended partly on the [[prestige|prestige]] of fine printing: a purchased greeting need not look carelessly chosen.

Behind these tender images stood demanding industrial processes. For engraved designs, workers could [[submerge|submerge]] prepared metal plates in acid, which ate into exposed lines. Printing machinery required regular [[lubrication|lubrication]], while accurate colour registration rewarded [[dogged|dogged]] persistence. As the trade expanded, manufacturers could [[affiliate|affiliate]] with trade associations. The apparently private exchange of affection thus rested on increasingly organised networks of skilled labour.

By the late nineteenth century, albums allowed recipients to preserve cards rather than discard them. Humorous illustrations might show children who [[sprawl|sprawled]] across a rug, replacing ceremonial dignity with recognisable domestic ease. Yet the printed message rarely eliminated handwriting altogether: a name, a date, or one additional sentence made the object particular. Mass production had not abolished intimacy; it had supplied a new surface on which to inscribe it.
zh: 在商业贺卡普及之前，节日里的情意主要通过手写书信传递。无论是致信远房堂表亲的商人，还是写信回家的传教士，都可能花上不少时间斟酌合适的称呼。这类通信颇费心力，但其私人性质也使它在情感表达上更有分量。此后贺卡的发展，始终围绕着一个问题：印刷文字能否保留这种亲密感。
在英国，邮资下降加快了这一转变。1843年受委托制作的那张著名圣诞贺卡，描绘了一家人围桌举杯的场景，两侧则是施舍救济的画面。后来的制造商推出了更加精巧的产品，浮雕边框与细腻着色都需要极其细致的制作。这些贺卡的吸引力部分来自精美印刷所享有的声望：买来的祝福，也未必显得是随便挑选的。
这些温情图像的背后，是要求严苛的工业工序。制作蚀刻图案时，工人可以将处理过的金属版浸入酸液，让酸液腐蚀裸露的线条。印刷机械需要定期润滑，而精确的彩色套印则有赖于坚持不懈的努力。随着行业扩张，制造商可以加入行业协会。由此，看似私密的情感交流，实际上依托着组织日益完善的熟练劳动力网络。
到了十九世纪末，人们可以将收到的贺卡收入集册，保存下来，而不是丢弃。诙谐的插图可能画着四肢摊开躺在地毯上的孩子，以熟悉的居家自在取代礼仪性的庄重。然而，印好的祝福语很少完全取代手写文字：一个名字、一个日期，或补写的一句话，就能使这件物品变得独一无二。批量生产并没有消除亲密感，而是为人们提供了一个承载它的新载体。

q.s: The personal nature of early seasonal letters contributed to their emotional significance.
q.why: 首段指出书信的私人性质赋予其情感分量。

q.s: Cheaper postage slowed the transition to greeting cards in Britain.
q.why: 第二段说较低邮资加快了这一转变。

q.s: Recipients usually arranged the cards in their albums by date.
q.why: 末段未说明集册中的贺卡如何排序。
